body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in two opinion pieces, judging whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence relevant and sufficient (RI.9-10.8).
- Students determine each author's purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it (RI.9-10.6), citing strong textual evidence (RI.9-10.1).
- Students write an argument with a precise claim, fair counterclaims, cohesive transitions and a formal style, drawing evidence from a source (W.9-10.1, W.9-10.1.a, W.9-10.1.b, W.9-10.1.c, W.9-10.1.d).
- Students write an argument on demand in a single sitting (W.9-10.10, W.9-10.1.e).

MATERIALS
- The readings "Let Teenagers Sleep: Start High School at 8:30" and "A Later Bell Is Not a Free Lunch" (in Anatomy of an Argument)
- The district brief on a community service requirement (in Should Community Service Be Required to Graduate?)
- The fact sheet on phones in class (in the on-demand argument)
- Two colors of highlighter or digital highlighting: one for claims, one for evidence
- A claim-evidence-reasoning organizer (three columns) and sentence-starter cards

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Argument That Persuades together. Quick-write: describe a time someone changed your mind. Model the four parts with a short spoken argument about a school lunch rule. Begin Anatomy of an Argument with the first opinion piece; students highlight the claim and each piece of evidence.
Day 2: Finish Anatomy of an Argument with the second piece. In pairs, students fill a two-column chart comparing evidence, then discuss: which piece has more sufficient evidence, and which uses more emotional appeal? Share out; collect the problem set.
Day 3: Launch Should Community Service Be Required to Graduate? Read the district brief as a class, marking facts versus opinions. Students choose a position (including the middle option) and draft a precise claim. Teacher conferences on claims while students outline.
Day 4: Drafting workshop. Mini-lesson on counterclaims: state the strongest opposing argument fairly, concede what is true, then rebut. Students draft the counterclaim paragraph first, then the body. Peer review with the rubric's four criteria. (Students finish and revise the essay over the following week.)
Day 5: Assessment: On-Demand Argument: Phones in Class. Students read the fact sheet and write in one period with no AI help. Collect and score with the rubric; note common gaps for a mini-lesson next week.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide the claim-evidence-reasoning organizer and starters ("This evidence matters because...", "Some argue that... However..."). Let students annotate one op-ed with a partner before working alone.
- Support: for the essay, offer a paragraph frame (claim, two reasons with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion) and a 300-word floor while students build stamina.
- Stretch: ask students to argue for the brief's middle option and explain why it is stronger than both extremes, or to evaluate how the survey's limitation (correlation, not causation) weakens or strengthens each side.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach claim, evidence, reasoning, counterclaim and rebut with visuals and home-language cognates (Spanish: evidencia, argumento). Allow students to plan in their home language and draft in English. Pair with a supportive partner for the op-ed reading, and accept bullet-point answers on the lesson.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit your student is learning to read and write arguments: a clear claim, evidence, reasoning, and a fair look at the other side. Their essay asks whether community service should be required to graduate. Ask your student which side they chose, and then ask them to tell you the best argument against their own position. If they can explain it fairly, they are on their way to a strong essay.
title: Teacher guide: The Power of Argument
